question_en: A company wants to use AWS to scale up the number of its long-running critical simulations. The company wants to perform large-scale parallel simulations that run for days. The simulations cannot be stopped. The company must store the output for later review by using durable and fault-tolerant storage. The output includes structured and unstructured data. The structured data includes simulation results. The unstructured data includes images up to 1 MB in size. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use AWS Lambda functions to perform simulations. Store structured data in Amazon RDS. Store unstructured data in Amazon S3.
options.B: Use AWS Batch to perform simulations. Store structured data in Amazon RDS. Store unstructured data in Amazon S3.
options.C: Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to perform simulations. Store structured data in Amazon RDS. Store unstructured data in Amazon DynamoDB.
options.D: Use AWS Batch to perform simulations. Store all data in an Amazon EBS volume.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Batch designed for long-running parallel simulations—manages job scheduling, compute environments, queues. RDS provides durable, fault-tolerant relational storage for structured simulation results. S3 offers highly durable (11 nines) object storage for unstructured images. Reliable capacity for non-interruptible jobs.

why_wrong.A: Lambda 15-minute maximum execution time insufficient for simulations running days. Can't use Lambda for long-running workloads.
why_wrong.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted—violates 'cannot be stopped' requirement. DynamoDB 400KB item limit potentially inadequate for simulation data.
why_wrong.D: Single EBS volume not durable shared storage across parallel workers. EBS single-AZ—lacks fault tolerance for critical data.

explanation.exam_tips: For long-running parallel compute: AWS Batch (not Lambda <15 min). For non-interruptible: avoid Spot (can interrupt). Structured data → RDS, unstructured → S3. Lambda max 15 min, Batch for days.
explanation.memorize: Long parallel simulations = AWS Batch + RDS (structured) + S3 (unstructured)

question_en: A company runs a non-production application on an Amazon EC2 instance that has the Amazon CloudWatch agent installed. The CloudWatch agent monitors application processes and sends custom metrics to CloudWatch. The application has a critical bug that causes crashes that require an instance reboot. The company does not currently have the resources to address the bug, but the server needs to remain as operational as possible. The company manually reboots the instance several times each day. The company needs a solution to automate the instance reboots until the company can address the root cause of the bug. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?

options.A: Use a CloudWatch alarm state change event to invoke Amazon EventBridge to run AWS Systems Manager Run Command to restart the instance.
options.B: Use a CloudWatch alarm to invoke an AWS Lambda function to run AWS Systems Manager Run Command to restart the instance.
options.C: Use a CloudWatch alarm to invoke an Amazon SNS topic that notifies the operations team to restart the instance.
options.D: Use a CloudWatch alarm to invoke an AWS Lambda function that automatically notifies the company through chat to restart the instance.

explanation.why_correct: CloudWatch alarm state changes se publican automáticamente a EventBridge. EventBridge puede invocar Systems Manager Run Command para reiniciar instancias EC2 remotamente. Esta solución es completamente serverless, sin código custom Lambda, mínima overhead operacional y usa servicios nativos AWS.

why_wrong.B: Funcional pero agrega Lambda innecesario. Menos eficiente que integración directa EventBridge → SSM Run Command. Más overhead operacional.
why_wrong.C: SNS requiere intervención humana para reiniciar. No cumple requisito de automatización.
why_wrong.D: Similar a C: notificación vía chat requiere acción manual. No automatiza el reinicio.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Least operational overhead' con automatización = servicios nativos integrados sin custom code. CloudWatch → EventBridge → SSM es patrón común. Lambda agrega overhead a menos que se requiera lógica custom.
explanation.memorize: CloudWatch alarm → EventBridge → SSM Run Command = reinicio automático sin Lambda.

question_en: A solutions architect needs to implement a solution that can handle up to 5,000 messages per second. The solution must publish messages as events to multiple consumers. The messages are up to 500 KB in size. The message consumers need to have the ability to use multiple programming languages to consume the messages with minimal latency. The solution must retain published messages for more than 3 months. The solution must enforce strict ordering of the messages.

options.A: Publish messages to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams data stream. Enable enhanced fan-out. Ensure that consumers ingest the data stream by using dedicated throughput.
options.B: Publish messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Ensure that consumers use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue to subscribe to the topic.
options.C: Publish messages to Amazon EventBridge. Allow each consumer to create rules to deliver messages to the consumer ' s own target.
options.D: Publish messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Ensure that consumers use Amazon Data Firehose to subscribe to the topic.

explanation.why_correct: Kinesis Data Streams supports 5K msgs/sec, 500KB messages, strict ordering per shard, 365-day retention. Enhanced fan-out for multiple consumers with dedicated throughput.

why_wrong.B: SNS doesn't enforce ordering. SQS FIFO 256KB limit, lower throughput.
why_wrong.C: EventBridge no ordering guarantees, 24-hour retention only.
why_wrong.D: SNS + Firehose batch-oriented, no strict ordering.

explanation.exam_tips: Kinesis = high throughput + ordering + long retention + multi-consumer. SQS FIFO = ordering but lower scale. Choose based on requirements.
explanation.memorize: Kinesis Data Streams = 5K msgs/sec + ordering + 365-day retention + enhanced fan-out.

question_en: A solutions architect is creating a data processing job that runs once daily and can take up to 2 hours to complete. If the job is interrupted, it has to restart from the beginning. How should the solutions architect address this issue in the MOST cost-effective manner?

options.A: Create a script that runs locally on an Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance that is triggered by a cron job.
options.B: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
options.C: Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Fargate task triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
options.D: Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task running on Amazon EC2 triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.

explanation.full_text: AWS Fargate with Amazon ECS is a serverless, fully managed compute engine for containers. Fargate eliminates the need to provision or manage servers, and is ideal for periodic, long-running batch jobs. You only pay for the resources consumed during job execution, making it cost-effective for jobs that run infrequently.
explanation.why_correct: Fargate supports up to 2 hours easily (no 15-min limit like Lambda). Serverless—no EC2 management. Pay-per-use pricing (per-second, 1-min minimum). EventBridge schedules daily execution. If interrupted, container restarts from beginning (requirement stated).

why_wrong.A: Reserved Instances require 1-3 year commitment for workload running once daily for 2 hours. Wastes 22 hours/day of paid capacity. RI optimizes for 24/7 workloads, not scheduled batch jobs.
why_wrong.B: Lambda maximum execution time = 15 minutes. Job takes up to 2 hours. Lambda would timeout and fail. Wrong compute service for long-running tasks.
why_wrong.D: ECS on EC2 requires provisioning, patching, and managing EC2 instances. Higher operational overhead than Fargate. Still pay for EC2 instance hours even when job not running (22hrs/day waste).

explanation.exam_tips: Job duration decision tree: <15min=Lambda, 15min-hours=Fargate, always-on=EC2. Scheduled batch jobs=serverless (Lambda/Fargate) to avoid idle costs. 'Restart from beginning if interrupted'=acceptable for both Fargate and EC2, but Fargate is cheaper for infrequent jobs.
memorize: Fargate: serverless containers, pay per vCPU-second and GB-second
Fargate minimum billing: 1 minute per task
Reserved Instances: 1 or 3 year commitment, for predictable 24/7 workloads
EventBridge Scheduler: free for first 14M invocations/month

question_en: A company needs to design a solution to process videos that users upload to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each video file is approximately 1 GB in size and takes approximately 20 minutes to process. During peak hours, the company expects to process approximately 100 simultaneous uploads. The video file processing is stateless and can run in parallel as soon as the video files arrive in the S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Use an AWS Lambda function to process each video. Split the video files into chunks, and use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate multiple processing steps.
options.B: Use an Amazon EKS cluster with AWS Fargate profiles to deploy one container for each uploaded video. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke the cluster when a user uploads a video.
options.C: Use Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group to process each file. Configure the Auto Scaling policy to increase the number of instances based on the number of files that the application needs to process.
options.D: Use an Amazon ECS cluster with the AWS Fargate launch type. Use Fargate Spot capacity to run one container task for each uploaded video. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke the cluster when a user uploads a video.

explanation.full_text: ECS on Fargate Spot runs event-driven container tasks at up to 70% discount. EventBridge triggers task per uploaded video.
explanation.why_correct: 20-minute processing = exceeds Lambda 15-min limit. Fargate = serverless containers, no instance management. Fargate Spot = up to 70% discount vs Fargate On-Demand. EventBridge = triggers ECS RunTask on S3 upload event. Pay only for 100 * 20 min = 33 hours/day during peak. Spot acceptable for stateless video processing (can retry if interrupted).

why_wrong.A: Lambda max execution = 15 minutes. Video processing = 20 minutes. Lambda would timeout and fail. 'Split into chunks + Step Functions' = major architectural change, adds complexity, still hits Lambda limits for large files.
why_wrong.B: EKS = Kubernetes, more operational overhead than ECS. Correct use of Fargate but EKS complexity unnecessary for simple parallel task pattern. ECS simpler for event-driven single-task workloads.
why_wrong.C: EC2 On-Demand Auto Scaling = managing instances. Always-on minimum capacity vs serverless pay-per-use. More expensive than Fargate Spot. Operational overhead (AMIs, patching, scaling policies).

explanation.exam_tips: '> 15 minutes' = exclude Lambda. 'Stateless parallel container' = Fargate. 'Cost-effective container' = Fargate Spot. ECS vs EKS: ECS = simpler, AWS-native; EKS = Kubernetes portability. EventBridge → ECS RunTask = standard event-driven pattern.
memorize: Fargate Spot: up to 70% discount, 2-minute termination notice
Fargate pricing: per vCPU-second + per GB-second
ECS: simpler, integrated; EKS: Kubernetes, portable

question_en: A solutions architect runs a web application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances that are in individual target groups behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Users can reach the application through a public website. The solutions architect wants to allow engineers to use a development version of the website to access one specific development EC2 instance to test new features for the application. The solutions architect wants to use an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone to give the engineers access to the development instance. The solution must automatically route to the development instance even if the development instance is replaced. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an A record for the development website that has the value set to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB that forwards requests for the development website to the target group that contains the development instance.
options.B: Recreate the development instance with a public IP address. Create an A record for the development website that has the value set to the public IP address of the development instance.
options.C: Create an A record for the development website that has the value set to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB to redirect requests for the development website to the public IP address of the development instance.
options.D: Place all the instances in the same target group. Create an A record for the development website. Set the value to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB that forwards requests for the development website to the target group.

explanation.why_correct: Route 53 A record points development hostname to ALB (stable endpoint). ALB listener rule matches development hostname and forwards to dedicated target group containing development instance. When instance replaced, target group simply registers new instance. DNS unchanged, automatic routing continuity.

why_wrong.B: Public IP changes when instance replaced, breaking DNS resolution. Requires manual DNS update.
why_wrong.C: ALB can't redirect to instance public IP directly. Architectural mismatch.
why_wrong.D: All instances in same target group means all receive development traffic, not just development instance.

explanation.exam_tips: For stable DNS to specific instance: Route 53 to ALB + listener rule + dedicated target group. Target group handles instance replacement automatically. Don't use public IPs (change on replacement).
explanation.memorize: Stable dev access + instance replacement = A record + ALB + listener rule + target group

question_en: An international company needs to share data from an Amazon S3 bucket to employees who are located around the world. The company needs a secure solution to provide employees with access to the S3 bucket. The employees are already enrolled in AWS IAM Identity Center. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

question_en: A company is building a cloud-based application on AWS that will handle sensitive customer data. The application uses Amazon RDS for the database. Amazon S3 for object storage, and S3 Event Notifications that invoke AWS Lambda for serverless processing. The company uses AWS IAM Identity Center to manage user credentials. The development, testing, and operations teams need secure access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3 while ensuring the confidentiality of sensitive customer data. The solution must comply with the principle of least privilege. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use IAM roles with least privilege to grant all the teams access. Assign IAM roles to each team with customized IAM policies defining specific permission for Amazon RDS and S3 object access based on team responsibilities.
options.B: Enable IAM Identity Center with an Identity Center directory. Create and configure permission sets with granular access to Amazon RDS and Amazon S3. Assign all the teams to groups that have specific access with the permission sets.
options.C: Create individual IAM users for each member in all the teams with role-based permissions. Assign the IAM roles with predefined policies for RDS and S3 access to each user based on user needs. Implement IAM Access Analyzer for periodic credential evaluation.
options.D: Use AWS Organizations to create separate accounts for each team. Implement cross-account IAM roles with least privilege Grant specific permission for RDS and S3 access based on team roles and responsibilities.
